analysis.one_liner: Exempts small, marginally producing oil and gas wells from EPA methane pollution rules.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on December 10, 2018, where it died without a hearing or vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have exempted low-producing oil and gas wells from the EPA's 2016 methane rule, which requires oil and gas operations to find and fix leaks of methane and other air pollutants. It covered any oil well averaging no more than 15 barrels of oil per day and any gas well averaging no more than 90,000 cubic feet per day over a 12-month period, including all emissions sources tied to those wells. The bill was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of marginally producing oil and gas wells, who would no longer have to comply with federal leak-detection and emissions-control requirements, lowering their compliance costs. These are typically older, lower-volume wells where control equipment is costly relative to production.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small oil and gas well operators

how_it_helps.text: The bill would exempt oil wells averaging 15 barrels per day or less and gas wells averaging 90,000 cubic feet per day or less from EPA's methane emissions standards and its Control Techniques Guidelines for the oil and gas industry.
The exemption would also cover any emission source associated with those qualifying wells, not just the wells themselves.

analysis.who_pays: People living near exempt wells and the general public would bear the cost of unchecked methane and smog-forming emissions, in the form of worse local air quality and added greenhouse gas pollution, since the federal standards would no longer apply to those sites.

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave emissions from exempt wells unregulated under these federal standards, because it covers not only the wells but every associated emissions source, meaning leaks and vents at those sites could go undetected and unrepaired.

Low-producing wells are numerous across older oil and gas regions, so a broad exemption could allow a substantial share of the industry's sites to operate outside the rule even as the rule stays on the books for larger producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: compliance equipment is expensive relative to output on marginal wells. But its remedy removes the emissions requirements entirely rather than easing them, shifting the health and climate costs of unchecked leaks onto nearby residents and the public. Given its zero cosponsors, the bill drew little support even among its potential beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 10, 2018 by Rep. Glenn Thompson of Pennsylvania.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's methane standards and Control Techniques Guidelines remain on the books for all wells, including marginal ones, so nearby communities kept the leak-detection protections the bill would have removed. No one gained, but the relief sought by low-producing well operators never arrived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near wells; the rule survived

for.name: Rep. Glenn Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt marginally producing oil and gas wells from EPA's methane rule.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of where parties stood.

industries.industry: Low-producing (marginal) oil and gas well operators
industries.note: The bill would have freed these operators from federal methane leak-detection and emissions-control costs. Because it died, they remain covered by the EPA standards and continue to bear compliance costs. [S3][S1]
Larger producers were not covered by the exemption and were unaffected either way; the broader industry's obligations under the 2016 methane rule were unchanged. [S3]
